A 19th-century academic oil painting with a smooth, finely blended surface: soft glazed transitions, delicate fine detail, minimal visible brushstrokes, no heavy impasto, no rough texture. Strong light and shadow from a single warm source (a lamp, a torch, a fire, a low sun) or from heavy overcast, with deep chiaroscuro. Palette of umber, ochre, gold, olive and near-black, with occasional cool accents. The manner of a romantic landscape, a grand historical scene, or a natural-history study of a creature painted as if real. A low, close viewpoint. Wet, reflective stone where there is stone; ancient architecture where there is architecture; one saturated subject held against darkness; scale shown by something small beside something vast. Quiet, watchful, ominous mood. No text, no lettering, no border, no frame, no grid texture, not photographic.

A grand historical scene inside a long, low hall with clay walls and a reed roof, on a mild morning in early autumn, seen from low at the end of a plain wooden bench. The only light is the low sun through the hall's one open door, which falls along the bench and leaves the roof and the far wall in near-black. On the bench stand eleven small weights of grey fired clay in a row, graded from the smallest to the largest, each casting a long shadow. At the end of the bench stands the one figure the light reaches fully. A tall, lean figure in a long coat with many deep pockets, the coat the first thing seen. The face is a middle-aged mortal's, plain, with steady eyes that watch as a man watches a scale while the pans settle. The hands are stained with ink and green verdigris. A pair of small, plain brass scales, slightly dented, hangs at the belt. Seen from behind or in deep shadow, the head turned away or lost in darkness, no face visible. Here the figure stands with its back to the viewer and the light on the long coat, holding the small brass scales up in one stained hand, the smallest clay weight lying in one pan and the pans settling. Beside the figure a grey-haired, unhurried man stands with his hand resting on the bench, watching the pans. At the bench's end a woman sits with a knife and a long split stick, cutting a notch. Along the dark wall behind them people sit on the floor in a ring, half seen. The hall is the inside of the long house of this place, and the open door looks out on its yard: A gate on the top of a high clay bank: two timber posts and a lintel standing alone, with no wall and no fence on either side, the gate open. Beyond it a yard of beaten clay, and a long, low house with clay walls and a reed roof, the largest roof in the town, its one door facing the yard. To one side of the yard a drum as wide as a cart wheel hangs on a frame of heavy timber. Through the door, far off and small in the bright daylight, a crowd stands waiting in the yard. The single small clay weight in the brass pan, beside the long dark hall and the waiting crowd, gives the scale. No stone buildings, no walls of stone, no armor, no weapons.
